items.followUp: Why does sweating cool the body?

rubric.why: Evaporation preferentially removes the faster, higher-energy molecules from the liquid.
rubric.description: Explains which molecules evaporate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that higher-energy or faster molecules escape during evaporation.

rubric.why: The remaining liquid loses average kinetic energy, or absorbs heat from its surroundings, so it cools.
rubric.description: Explains why the remaining liquid becomes cooler.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking evaporation to reduced average kinetic energy or heat absorption and cooling.

modelAnswer: During evaporation, the higher-energy molecules escape from the surface of the liquid.
The average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules decreases, so the liquid absorbs heat from its surroundings and cools.
Thus, evaporation is a cooling process.
A similar example is the cooling effect of sweat evaporating from the skin.

items.followUp: Define percentage by mass (% m/m) and write its formula.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the volume of solute compared with the total volume of solution.
rubric.description: Identifies the quantities used in % v/v.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the volume of solute per volume of solution.

rubric.why: The formula expresses the volume ratio as a percentage.
rubric.description: Gives the correct formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ratio of solute volume to solution volume multiplied by 100.

modelAnswer: Percentage by volume (% v/v) is the volume of solute present in 100 volumes of solution.
% v/v = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100

items.followUp: State the Bohr postulates that explain the emission of a spectral line.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy specific permitted orbits with definite energies.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy permitted orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for identifying fixed permitted orbits and their definite energies.

rubric.why: An electron in a permitted orbit does not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating that electrons do not radiate or lose energy while remaining in an orbit.

rubric.why: Radiation is emitted or absorbed when an electron moves between energy levels, with energy equal to their difference.
rubric.description: Explains emission or absorption during an electron transition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating an electron transition to emitted or absorbed energy equal to the difference between levels.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted circular orbits called energy levels or shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher energy level and emits energy when it moves to a lower energy level.
The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the two energy levels: ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Write any four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas a mixture can have variable proportions.
rubric.description: Compares composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-versus-variable composition difference.

rubric.why: The substances in a compound are chemically combined; those in a mixture are physically mixed.
rubric.description: Compares how the substances are combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chemical-combination versus physical-mixing difference.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituent elements, while mixture components retain their properties.
rubric.description: Compares the properties of the constituents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct difference in properties.

rubric.why: Compounds are separated chemically, while mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: Compares methods of separation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chemical-versus-physical separation difference.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition; a mixture can have a variable composition.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined; the substances in a mixture are physically mixed.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; substances in a mixture retain their properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.

items.followUp: Explain why water molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen attached to a highly electronegative atom, commonly N, O, or F.
rubric.description: Identifies the hydrogen bond donor arrangement.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating that hydrogen is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as oxygen, nitrogen, or fluorine.

rubric.why: The hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair or negative region on a nearby electronegative atom.
rubric.description: Explains the intermolecular attraction involved.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for describing the attraction between hydrogen and a nearby electronegative atom or its lone pair.

rubric.why: A suitable example and identification of the bond as an intermolecular attraction complete the explanation.
rubric.description: Gives an example or identifies hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example such as water, or for identifying it as an intermolecular force.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular electrostatic attraction involving a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F.
The hydrogen atom is attracted to a lone pair or partial negative charge on an electronegative atom in a nearby molecule.
For example, hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring water (H₂O) molecules.
Hydrogen bonding is weaker than a covalent bond.
